utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning to the technical booth and the interpreters; good morning to the Office of the Prosecutor, the Defence counsel; good morning, General Krstic. We're now going to resume with the testimony of Mr. Rudovic, and when we finish that questioning, we will take up with the questions of the General. We are now going to have Mr. Rudovic introduced into court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Rudovic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you feel well? Everything all right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sure you'll be able to answer questions put to you by Mr. Petrusic. I think we were still with the year 1992, and I think we ought to move on, speed things up a bit. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, my learned colleagues of the Prosecution, and everybody else in court. I think we'll get through 1992 and 1995 very quickly this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Petrusic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rudovic, you left off yesterday telling us in your testimony when you met General Krstic and I think that was at the beginning of 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what was the conversation you had with the General who was then a Lieutenant Colonel, Krstic, Commander of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade, which was the brigade to which you yourself belonged to at the time?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say first of all that I was very nervous yesterday. But as to our conversation, with the leader of my company, I went to Lieutenant Colonel Krstic, to Gusinac, which is where he was, he had a sort of tent there, and he explained to us what safe area meant, what we had the right to, what they had the right to do, what their rights were, what our rights were, and he informed us about the line. He said that they had been disarmed and we were not allowed to engage in any provocations; that we were Serbian soldiers, that we must respect the image of us as soldiers. As I said, my brother's son was killed and my son was killed as well, and lots of other people killed. Many people were killed and expelled and forced to leave. But he told me that I must be a true Serbian soldier and live up to that image and that I must not do anything. When I raised my voice, he said, "No, I don't want Serbian soldiers of that kind in my army," and what I told him was the following: "You're saying the same thing that the priest told me at my son's funeral: No eye for an eye or tooth for a tooth. That is definitely not allowed." That's what the priest told me during the funeral of my son.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Lieutenant Krstic told you at the time that you must be a real, true Serbian soldier?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me finish, please. Without any acts of revenge or undertaking any acts of that kind towards the Muslim army or the civilian population. And that, as far as I was able to understand your testimony, that he didn't want the likes of you in the Serbian army because he did not want to be responsible for any war crimes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Briefly speaking, Mr. Rudovic, tell us, please, when the safe area was set up, did you respect the rules and regulations governing a safe area, a protected area?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the time I was at Zepa, and we respected the whole front line, the whole line all the time. There were no provocations from either side. But I must say that from the other side there were provocations. First of all, they had not been disarmed, as we were told, and they would hit us -- come from the rear, behind our back. The line was 35, 40 kilometres. They would cross the line. They had 4 or 5 kilometres of no-man's land in between, and they would kill the population there. They would seize the cattle, the livestock, and they would lay an ambush for the army and they would ambush the drivers taking food, driving food, or ambulances or things of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so at the beginning of that year, 1993, when the safe area was established, was formed, it moved from within the composition of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade to the 65th Motorised Regiment, Protection Regiment; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were a member of the battalion of that 65th Protection Regiment?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of a battalion of the Protection Regiment until 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that an infantry battalion?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was an infantry battalion with light weaponry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And within that structure you had your company leader and Battalion Commander, I assume.

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we had a Battalion Commander, leader of the company, a Commander of the platoon. It was a proper unit organised as it should be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Petrusic, the interpreters have asked us to ask you to make a pause between question and answer. You two are speaking the same language, but, Witness, there is always an interpreter, and unless you make breaks, it won't be possible. And if you go on that way, it will be just a conversation between the two of you and nobody else will benefit. So please pay attention to that, Mr. Petrusic, and I do think that Mr. Petrusic did caution you, Witness, when you started your testimony. But that is not a criticism. I should just like to ask you to do that. We don't understand your language so try and speak as slowly as possible and make pauses between you and Mr. Petrusic. Having said that, Mr. Petrusic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rudovic, at the beginning of July 1995, where were you; that is to say, where was your unit located?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were on the same line at which we were located in 1992. We had a pause, a break. We shifted -- we moved for the winter, then they expanded that zone, then we had to return to our former positions where we were in 1992, so we stayed there until the end of 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you at that position when the combat actions in 1995 began, that is to say, on the 14th of July, at Zepa?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there throughout. I was there the whole time until the fall of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, during the combat at Zepa, that is to say, from the 14th of July, if you know, what was the chain of command in your unit? Who did you receive your orders from?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The company leader. Company leaders would issue orders, and probably they received their orders from the Battalion Commander, and that's how the line goes, the chain goes. He was the leader of the company --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the leader of the company after the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The company leader was Gojko Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking about the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was killed then and he was replaced by the Dragan Kosoric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the Battalion Commander?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Battalion Commander up until then was Milanko Beatovic, but he was later replaced sometime in 1994 by Radivojevic. I don't know his name. And he was there until the end, he was in that post until the end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you happen to know who your Battalion Commander received orders from?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably from the higher commanding officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May we then say that you don't have any precise knowledge in that direction?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean who he received them from?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, your Commander.

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were several officers. For example, in our sector of the line, the unit I was in, it belonged to the 2nd Romanija and to the Protection Platoon because it was all mixed up. Now if I were to begin to tell you all that, well -- we were told that we ought to be on the ready because in Zepa all the UNPROFOR soldiers had been disarmed. And then provocations started and that is when I felt the first fighting of 1992. They killed Gojko Petrusic, our company leader, and wounded a soldier, and that's how the operation was launched, that's how it started. And there was Colonel Andric there and there was Krstic, I think he was still a Lieutenant Colonel at the time, and they were up at Borica, to the right of us, up there. And I heard about him when he passed from Zepa, Tolimir. I don't know what his name was. Miroslav, maybe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rudovic, tell us, during that period, from the 14th of July up until the fall of Zepa, did you have any prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our company, we had two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you did with them?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there they are today, alive and well. One of the men's name was Osman Omerspahic, and he went to prison straight away. We turned him over to the police and the police held him in custody. He was exchanged. And there he is today, driving a bus from Sarajevo to Gorazde. And he is a local of Han Pijesak and he doesn't even pay his bus tickets to anybody when he gets on a bus -- he doesn't charge for bus rides. So when Zepa fell later on, there was another one and his name was Ramic, and he went to Sarajevo to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During those combat activities at Zepa from the 14th of July to the 2nd of August, did you have occasion to see General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw General Krstic on two occasions, at the beginning and at the end, that is to say, at the beginning when we moved out to Zepa, and when the whole operation finished, I saw them. That's where we parted ways. And I went home. Whether he left before me, I don't know, because everybody has his own road to follow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us about a detail from your meeting, you described a detail from your meeting that was at the beginning of April/May 1993, and it was about the way he criticised you and told you how you must behave as a soldier, what your conduct should be.

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't say that to me, he told the whole army. He explained the importance of the line, the importance of the safe area, the importance of the fact that they had been disarmed, and the role of UNPROFOR. And that was -- they separated us. There were 2 kilometres from their line to our lines, and that was a sort of no-man's land, a space in between. They were always over there. They never came over here, only if they came by official vehicles. So they didn't pass -- the UNPROFOR men didn't pass on to our line, and that's how we held those lines. That's how it was until they were disarmed. Once they were disarmed, then they were impotent and they asked for protection. One checkpoint was somewhere up by Borica and it was at that checkpoint there, there were 12 of them who had been captured because they were nearer to the Serb positions, so that that was how it was. And all their weapons, all the weapons that they seized they used against us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're talking about the Muslim side, are you?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Muslims captured them, they took their weapons, and then they used those weapons to strike against us. Krstic -- well, I've told you already. Krstic held that line until we moved to the protection regiment, and he advised us how we should -- what our conduct should be, that we should be real fighters, that we mustn't touch civilians or anybody who is injured or anybody who surrenders. We were not allowed to do anything to them or shoot at them or anything. That's what I'm telling you. Now, what can you do if you're not allowed to shoot? But that was how it was and we respected that up at that line there. And 2 or 3 kilometres along the line they tilled the land which was on our territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Could you slow down, please, now.

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They worked the land, their own land, which was in fact on our territory, but they did not carry weapons at that time. They would sow and reap and so on. But nobody touched them. They went about their business and that was how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence has no further questions for Mr. Rudovic. That completes his testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I haven't said something that I wanted to say. When we got down during all that time, when my leader was killed, we advanced several kilometres, and then they made trenches on our in the course of the night and launched their operations from there. When our leader was killed we came to those trenches and took control of those trenches, but they said that there were to be negotiations and the negotiations went on for a day or two, I don't know actually how long, but they did not succeed. And then we advanced again. They attacked us; we advanced again, because as soon as the negotiations failed there was shooting straight away and that's what we had to do. And I spent about four -- I spent five or six days doing those 4 or 5 kilometres. And when we got down there, when Zepa surrendered, the Serb soldiers did not go into Zepa until the last civilian had left, and they all left single-file in buses by us, because we had control of the road. And I know that today that there is the president of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting you, Mr. Rudovic. Mr. Petrusic did say that he did not have any more questions for you. We all know that you would have many, many, things to tell us, and you are going to tell us in answering the questions put to you by Mr. Andrew Cayley. I hope I haven't changed his name. He's going to ask you questions. Are you ready to do that? Are you ready and willing to answer questions by Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am. I'm quite ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Mr. Cayley, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning. Good morning to my learned friends. I have very few questions, actually, for the witness. Cross-examined by Mr. Cayley:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Rudovic. First of all, please accept on behalf of myself and my colleagues profound regret at the loss of your son and nephew during this war. I would like to direct your mind to Zepa and July of 1995, and I have very few questions and it concerns a matter that you just mentioned, the evacuation of the civilians from Zepa. If you don't know the answers to the questions I ask you, you can simply say to the Judges that you don't know. First of all, after the fall of Zepa, did you ever hear of the removal from a bus of 36 Muslims, including wounded individuals, by Serb forces? Did you ever hear about that? These were Bosniak soldiers being evacuated from Zepa. Did you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand the question. I never heard about that, nor did that happen where we were, anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear, Witness, that after the fall of the enclave and Zepa, that the Bosniak Commander, Colonel Avdo Palic, was murdered? Did you ever hear about that incident?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard that he was murdered. I don't know. I know Palic, I knew him from before the war, but I never heard that he was murdered. He was declared missing, that's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear, after the fall of Zepa and still to this day, that there are 118 missing Muslim men from the Zepa enclave? Did you ever hear about that? These are men who disappeared in July of 1995; they've never been seen again.

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard that. I don't know. Our former neighbours come by, and I never heard from any one of them that someone was missing. But probably there are some of them in Australia and they don't want to report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I won't read it out to the witness. I direct you to Prosecutor's Exhibit 30, paragraphs 425 onwards. This is the report of the Secretary-General to the General Assembly on the fall of Zepa that discusses these matters. I have no further questions for the witness. Thank you very much, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, have you any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Judge Fouad Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Judge Wald, no? Mr. Rudovic, I also have no questions for you. I would just like to say that I hope you will, for many years to come, benefit from the advantages that you have, the small benefits such as travelling to Sarajevo without paying a ticket. So we wish you a safe return home and thank you very much for coming here, Mr. Rudovic. The usher is going to escort you out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it would be better to have a short ten-minute break so that General Krstic can prepare and take his seat in the witness box. So we're going to have a short, ten-minute break. --- Break taken at 9.48 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Krstic, good morning. Are you feeling well?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Better, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will now resume with our questions. You will remember that we were talking about the procedure of the transmission of orders coming from the Commander-in-Chief when those orders are expected to be carried out by a unit of a brigade. So could you remind us of that procedure and how it worked.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that orders can be issued in writing to subordinate officers and units, and also orally. A written order is a customary form of issuing orders and orders are most frequently issued in that way. They may be transmitted by code or by handing the written order to the command of the subordinate unit or to the Commander of the subordinate unit. Oral orders are most frequently issued on the spot to the commanding officer whose unit is to carry out the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But an order coming from the Main Staff for a brigade, does it have to go through the Corps Commander. We are talking in general terms.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such cases were not frequent. Most frequently orders do pass through the command of the Corps, but they may be addressed directly to lower level subordinate units when we are talking about the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We stopped when we were talking about a specific order, Exhibit 709. We placed it under the ELMO at the time, the exhibit. I will give you some information about it. Perhaps it is not necessary to show it to you because you are familiar with it. That order is an order coming from the Main Staff and which mentioned specifically Captain Trpic - do you remember that order in connection with fuel - so that order was coming from the Main Staff for a brigade and made specific mention of Captain Trpic. Do you remember that order in connection with fuel? So that order was coming the Main Staff for a brigade and made specific mention of Captain Trpic. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you need to see it, to see the order?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, can you give us Exhibit 709. General Krstic, you have in front of you this order coming from the General Staff, signed by General Mladic. And as you can see, it is sent to a brigade and it mentions Captain Milorad Trpic. This order, according to the customary procedure, should it have gone through the Corps command or could it be addressed directly to this individual, Captain Milorad Trpic?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been addressed directly to that person. But from this order, it can be seen that it says: "Attention: Command of the Drina Corps," then the logistic sector of the General Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, for the information to the 1st Zvornik Infantry Brigade. So this is a logistics body of the Drina Corps command. And in this document, General Mladic specifies the tasks which that officer needs to carry out with approved quantities of fuel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, General Krstic, I'm sorry for interrupting you. So you have answered my question. Now let us look at the other side of the question. To whom should Captain Milorad Trpic report regarding the implementation of this order?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He must report to the person issuing the order, in this case General Ratko Mladic, because he is the one who is giving the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this a normal situation or an exceptional situation?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a possible situation. The rules and regulations do make provision for such a possibility, and in practice it may occur. So a higher level commanding officer is entitled to give orders to a lower level commanding officer as to what he should do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So let us now go on to another topic and another question. You spoke at length about the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You said that a large number, and there are documents, a large number of soldiers, and particularly officers, left the Srebrenica enclave beginning with July 1994 to join their families in Tuzla. Would you agree with that conclusion, with that statement?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did speak about that on the basis of documents of the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this was also visible throughout the period following the proclamation of the safe area of Srebrenica, that a certain number of members of the BH army left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you agree with that statement. My question is the following: Do you know whether those soldiers were able to join the 2nd Corps of the army in Tuzla, or in any event was that what the VRS thought they did?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The members of the 28th Division in the safe area of Srebrenica and Zepa did join the 2nd Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and also the 1st Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, whose area of responsibility was Sarajevo and the environs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know what exactly was the Operative Zone of the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Operative Zone of the 28th Division, from the beginning of the outbreak of hostilities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, covered the territories of the municipalities of -- and I'm saying until the proclamation of the safe area, the municipalities of Vlasenica, Sekovici, Zvornik, Bratunac, Milici, Srebrenica, a part of Han Pijesak municipality, specifically I'm referring to Zepa. So the whole of the area of Birac and central Podrinje and a part of upper Podrinje. When I'm saying "upper Podrinje," I'm thinking of Zepa, because Zepa belongs to the area of Gornja Podrinje. After the proclamation of Srebrenica and Zepa as safe areas, the area of responsibility of the 28th Division was the Srebrenica enclave and Zepa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know what were the effectives of the 28th Division was as a whole, what their strength was?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about that at some length, and I said that Srebrenica and Zepa were never demilitarised zones, even though they were proclaimed safe areas. And when those areas were declared safe areas, the 28th Division was still armed. They had infantry weapons at their disposal and also artillery weapons of a calibre up to 120-millimetres. And after Srebrenica and Zepa were proclaimed safe areas, the 28th Division continued to arm itself either by deliveries of weapons and ammunition from Tuzla, Kladanj, and Sarajevo, or those same weapons being delivered Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. by helicopter to the area of Srebrenica and Zepa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you are telling us coincides with the assessment of the situation that you made for the Operation Krivaja 95? Does that coincide? In other words, the number of troops present in Srebrenica and the quantity and quality of weaponry, are they what you have just said, or was there a change in the quality and quantity of troops and weapons for the Krivaja Operation?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any event, the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the areas of Zepa and Srebrenica were constantly organisationally promoting and modernising the division as a whole, and its effectives and strength was increasing and they were arming themselves additionally, which is not logical. Because if the area was proclaimed a safe area, why, then, should the 8th Operative Group be changed to the 28th Division? Because, after all, a division is a much stronger and more powerful unit than an operative group, and it has several brigades within it as well as independent units up to battalion strength.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mentioned that the attack on Srebrenica was launched with the aim of putting an end to sabotage operations engaged in by BH forces and a number of operations were mentioned; for example, operations which started in November 1994, the Operation Skakavac or Grasshopper, and you also mentioned the spring offensive. My question is the following: These three operations, are they one and the same operation with different stages or are they quite independent and separate operations?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any event, those operations were linked together. The Skakavac Operation was the introduction to the spring offensive by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the whole area. The Skakavac Operation consisted of sabotage activities, the aim of which was to engage in sabotage operations either in relation to members of the VRS or by incursions into villages and inflicting of casualties, creating an atmosphere of insecurity among the Serb population in the territory under the control of the Serbs; or more specifically, everything needed to be disorganised and undermined so as to create conditions that would be an introduction to a broader-scale operation, an operation of combat, which, with regard to the Drina Corps, was indeed launched in the spring of 1995, or to be more precise, in the middle and end of June 1995, launched from Tuzla towards Srebrenica, and from Kladanj towards Vlasenica, and also from the direction of Olovo towards Sokolac. The Operation Skakavac was under the direct command of the General Staff of the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina from their forward command post, I think, in Kakanj. In any event, all orders issued to the 28th Division were issued from that command post, and occasionally also from the command of the 2nd Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question, General Krstic: These operations, did they cover the whole territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina or did they apply solely to the eastern part of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army of Bosnia-Herzegovina started the spring offensive first on the Sarajevo theatre of war with a view to deblocking Sarajevo; and then along the Neretva River Valley towards the area of responsibility of the Herzegovina Corps; then towards the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps, that is, the eastern part of Bosnia-Herzegovina; and later we know that a broader-scale operation was carried out in western Bosnia-Herzegovina, when one-third of the territory under Serb control was taken over by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and placed under its control and that of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question, General Krstic: The report of the UN Secretary-General notes, and I'll read it in English, that: [In English] " The most substantial military operation conducted by the Bosniaks of Srebrenica during the safe area period was the right of Visnjica," dated the 26th of June, 1995. Do you agree with this judgement or assessment?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with the assessment. The main aim of the 28th Division, from the moment the safe areas were proclaimed, was for Srebrenica and Zepa to be physically linked and placed under the control of the 28th Division, and later on for that area, via Mount Javor, to be expanded towards Kladanj. The village of Visnjica lies there and also the area of the village of Banja Lucica, in the territory of the Han Pijesak municipality; then the area of the village of Rijecica, which is on the border between Han Pijesak municipality and Kladanj. So it was in this area that most of the operations of the 28th Division were carried out, operations of a diversionary and sabotage nature, and our population forces suffered the greatest casualties there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The report also explains that these operations had as their principal aim to deliver supplies to the enclaves, and also the report says 100 sheep were taken from Visnjica and were then eaten up. Would you agree with that description?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the aims, in addition to the armed -- to the military aims, was to supply foodstuffs. But it was not only the forces of the 28th Division that were short of food, they supplied also to the territories under Serb control, and there was a general shortage of food. So that the assistance that came from the International Community to the civilian population of all three sides was also used by the military because there was no other food to be found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, you said in your testimony that the Commander of the 28th Division, Naser Oric, was on his way to Tuzla on the 28th of June, 1995. When do you think that he came back from Sarajevo? And if you do know, how did you learn about it?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That the Commander of the 28th Division, General Naser Oric, left the safe area of Srebrenica was something that we learnt earlier on from intelligence reports, and we were later able to confirm this through the exhibits and the Muslim documents showing that he did, indeed, leave the area of Srebrenica and that he went outside that area. We were informed that with a large number of soldiers, members of the 28th Division, he first went to Sarajevo to take part in the spring offensive to deblock Sarajevo, and then later he was transferred to the territory of Tuzla, within the 2nd Corps of the BH army, which was in command of the forces in Srebrenica, the strength of one battalion, in the spring offensive towards Zvornik and Srebrenica. This was from the 15th of July onwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, General. I'd now like to go on to another set of questions. When the operation against Srebrenica was launched in 1995, did you know that a first offensive had already been launched against Srebrenica in 1993?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I was the Commander of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade, so this was not an offensive against Srebrenica but against the broader area of Birac, and I have in mind, in the first place, Cerska, Konjevic Polje, and Nova Kasaba. That operation was provoked by the activities of the 28th Division, mostly provoked by their activities in the territory between Bratunac and Konjevic Polje, a group of villages, Kravica and other villages surrounding Kravica. It was carried out -- or, rather, it started around the end of February, went on through March, and then also in April, when Srebrenica was declared a safe area. As I was saying, at that time I was the Commander of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade, and the Commander of that operation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry for interrupting you. So you mentioned that after that Srebrenica was declared a safe area. Did you know that one of the reasons for declaring it a safe area was precisely the shortage of supplies, of foodstuffs, medicines, and so on?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not known at the time that that was the reason why Srebrenica was declared a safe area. I understood it to be as protection of the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but when you participated in the planning of the Operation Krivaja 95, you already knew that this reason for declaring it a safe area was a determining factor, or not?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the shortage of food?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I did not know that that was the reason for the proclamation of Srebrenica as a safe area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When did you learn that the shortage of supplies was one of the reasons for declaring it a safe area?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not learn at all that that was the reason for proclaiming Srebrenica a safe area. I never learnt that. I said already that there were food shortages throughout the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina equally among all three sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Specifically, General Krstic, did you know that the first evacuation of Muslims from Srebrenica took place between March and April 1993?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have detailed information about that because I wasn't in the area. I was in the area around Kladanj, Olovo, and Vares.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry for interrupting you. You had no precise information? What type of information did you have regarding this first evacuation of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no information about the evacuation of Muslims. But it was visible that they were leaving the protected area partly through the area of responsibility of the 2nd Romanija Brigade, through the positions of the 2nd Romanija Brigade, towards Kladanj. That there was some kind of organised evacuation is something I never heard about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Something else. At that time, 1993, March/April, who was the Commander of the Drina Corps? I think I know the answer but I'd like to hear it from you.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ever since the Drina Corps was formed, until the 20th of July, 1995, that is, from November 1992 to the 20th of July, 1995, the Commander of the Drina Corps was General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Another set of questions. Did you also know that an operation was launched against the Gorazde enclave in April 1994 by General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this was in 1994 and not 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you are right. I was saying 1994.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You knew about this operation. Did you know what were the objectives of that operation?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I was still the Commander of the 2nd Romanija Brigade. That operation took place at a time when the BH army launched an operation from Kladanj towards the territory of the municipality of Han Pijesak and Vlasenica. I was not aware of the specific goals of that operation. It was under the command and control of General Mladic, and General Zivanovic was with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but in any event, General Krstic, now, taking into account the events we have discussed in 1993, Srebrenica, taking into account the events we referred to in Gorazde in 1994, do you see any difference or similarity between those operations and the Krivaja 95 Operation? Is it possible to establish a relationship between these three events: Srebrenica, 1993; Gorazde, 1994; Srebrenica, 1995?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, as far as I personally am concerned, bearing in mind the aim that was to have been achieved by Operation Krivaja 95, which was the physical separation of the two enclaves, so it has absolutely nothing in common with these other operations, 1994 in Birac, in central Podrinje, and the spring of 1994 towards Gorazde. This operation, Krivaja 95, was an operation of limited scope, very limited scope, to separate the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa and reach the lines that I have spoken about at length, and nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Perhaps I can put that question to you differently. In relation to the BH army or, rather, Bosnia-Herzegovina, the various operations that we have mentioned, Skakavac, the spring offensive, et cetera, were they one and the same or different operations? Now, let me put the question to you: In relation to an objective which I don't know - perhaps you do - Srebrenica 1993, Gorazde 1994, and Srebrenica 1995, were they operations quite distinct and independent from one another or are they related in relation to a particular objective of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are different areas quite far removed from one another. When we are talking about the operation of central Podrinje and Birac in the spring of 1993, the area of Gorazde in 1994, I really could not identify any similarities with respect to the objectives of those operations, because in 1993 and 1994 a war was raging in those areas. There were constant combat operations. Those combat operations were not ongoing only during the duration of those operations but they were going on continuously. There were battles, fighting, at lower levels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, General Krstic, would you at least agree with me in saying that General Mladic, the Chief of the Main Staff, and the Commander of the Drina Corps, General Zivanovic, they were present in several operations, or not?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we are talking about broader-scale operations, such as 1993, the spring of 1994, in both those areas, both the Commander of the Drina Corps, General Zivanovic, and the Commander of the Main Staff of the VRS, General Mladic, were present and they were in command and control of those operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me put another question to you, General Krstic. Who, in 1995, among the senior officers, participated also in the operation Srebrenica 1993 and possibly in the operation Gorazde 1994? We saw that Zivanovic and Mladic participated. Are there officers in 1995 who participated also in these other operations?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which senior officers in addition to General Zivanovic and General Mladic took part in the operations in 1993 and 1994. I really don't know because in those days I was a Brigade Commander. However, those same two senior officers were involved in the Operation Krivaja 95. Among the senior officers, I'm only aware of the presence of General Gvero on the 8th of July, 1995, and on the 9th, in the morning, at the forward command post at Pribicevac. So he is the only one among the senior officers, in addition to General Mladic and General Zivanovic, that were on the spot during the Krivaja 95 Operation while combat operations were ongoing. Whether General Gvero was also involved in the spring operations in 1993 and 1994 that you have referred to, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Very well. General, let us go on to another set of questions. You said that the former Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps, General Skocajic resigned in April of 1995 and that his resignation was motivated by a personal conflict with General Zivanovic. Did you know what the substance of that disagreement was, what it was about?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I found it strange that after I was wounded and after I left to the Military Medical Academy in Belgrade to be treated that General Skocajic, as the former Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps, was again called upon to carry out the duty of the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps. I learnt about that from people who came to visit me in hospital. General Skocajic is a highly educated officer who has graduated from all levels of military schools, the Military Academy, the Staff Academy, and the School of National Defence, and as such he was the Chief of Staff of General Zivanovic. I said that I was surprised that he could agree to go back to be Chief of Staff, which he was called to do by General Zivanovic through the Main Staff. In April 1995 he left that position allegedly because of a conflict with General Zivanovic. What I was able to hear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but the question is -- yes, yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I was able to learn, the main reason for him to leave that position was his disagreement with the method of control and command over the units of the Corps. Whether General Zivanovic and General Skocajic had some earlier differences when General Skocajic was the Chief of Staff of the Corps, I really wouldn't enter into that. But I have said what kind of conflict it was with respect to General Skocajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, General Krstic. You also said that you didn't consider yourself to be highly appreciated by General Mladic and General Zivanovic, especially when you were the Commander of the 2nd Romanija Brigade. You told us about that. You said that when they visited you it was a very brief visit, whereas when they visited others they stayed longer. My question: Did you continue to feel this later on, and particularly during the operations against Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about the relationship between General Zivanovic and myself, his relationship towards me, while I was the Commander of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade. Before that we never knew each other, that is true, nor had we seen each other. I don't know why this relationship was as it was, and perhaps this is not the place to say that. My mother is a refugee from the village where I was born. She received accommodation somewhere in Vlasenica, temporary accommodation. However, General Zivanovic, in a way, made used of his respect and influence on the structures in town, and she had to leave that makeshift accommodation she was given, although she had no where else to go. There are a series of other examples when it comes to his relationship towards me. There is a letter, for example, which he sent to the Commander of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska after I had come across the mine which blew my leg away, and in that letter I am represented in very bad terms; he writes about me in very bad terms. And General Zivanovic even went so far as to tell the commanding officer of my co-in-command that General Krstic was not left without a leg. That is not true, he did not lose a leg. There he is somewhere over there in Serbia, on one of the mountains of Serbia, in a recuperation place, whereas everybody knew that I had, in fact, lost a leg and was undergoing treatment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Allow me, General Krstic, to interrupt you at this point. I think that I am having some difficulties here. General Skocajic was replaced, according to you, because he didn't agree with how the Drina Corps' command was being exerted. You were not appreciated by General Mladic and General Zivanovic. Now, can we say that you were not appreciated but you were Chief of the Main Staff like General Skocajic because you agreed with the Commander and the way in which the Drina Corps' command was being exerted? Do you see my perplexities, the difficulties I'm having here?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to the relationship between Generals Skocajic and Zivanovic the same holds true for me. Perhaps I had done the same thing that General Skocajic had done, but I didn't have time for that because I was the Chief of Staff of the Corps for a very short period of time, for the reasons that I have talked at length about. There was the wounding, the injury, and I wasn't the Chief of Staff for even two or three months and I was not able to get to know Zivanovic, perhaps, well enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As Chief of Staff of the Main Staff, but you accepted to be Commander of the Drina Corps, so that means that for you that would have been an opportunity to exercise command in a different fashion than it had been exercised previously by General Zivanovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had to accept the post of Commander, Corps Commander; I had to do so. And as Brigade Commander, I commanded differently from General Zivanovic. And as the Corps Commander, I exercised my commanding duties in a different way from General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, excuse me for interrupting. But you said that you did not do, as Chief of the Main Staff, what General Skocajic did because you did not have time, and I can understand that. But why, then, accept -- you had the time not to accept to be Commander of the Corps, you had all the time to refuse.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, that was the situation, that was what the situation was like, that was what the time was like. Quite simply, the duties that I was assigned to I did not dare to refuse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Could General Zivanovic refuse to continue to be the Corps Commander? In a situation of war and an operation ongoing, could he have refused to continue until the end of the battle to be the Commander of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he could have refused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He could have refused.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He and General Mladic don't know each other, only from the army of Republika Srpska and during the duration of these operations. They have known each other for a much longer length of time, from the beginning of the war, from the outbreak of the conflict in the regions of the former Yugoslavia. They were together in Knin, for example, and then they came to Bosnia-Herzegovina together. And immediately after that, General Zivanovic, that is to say, after a certain period of time, was appointed Commander of the Corps. He was highly respected by General Mladic. And I see no reason why he should have refused to perform that function. He was, until the end of the fighting for part of Srebrenica and Zepa, he was there [As interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, General, perhaps it is a time for a break. You may be a little tired and you need a rest, and so do we. Perhaps we can have a break now, a half-hour break. Yes, Mr. Visnjic, before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this last sentence of General Krstic's, I think it is not correct in the transcript. General Krstic, I think, said that he was Commander until the end of the Srebrenica operation and part of the Zepa operation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was talking about General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, General Zivanovic was the Commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the transcript has now been corrected that General Krstic was talking about General Zivanovic. So we'll have a half-hour break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you ready to continue, General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we heard here in the courtroom a speech by President Radovan Karadzic underlining your merits for planning and successfully completing the Srebrenica operation. You explained that that speech did not correspond to reality but that it illustrated even more the bad relations that existed at the time between Karadzic and Mladic. Could you please specify the nature of those bad relations? And since when were they on bad terms?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult to talk about that. I think that an Assembly of Republika Srpska, whether it was held in Sanski Most or Prijedor, I'm not quite sure - I think it was in Sanski Most, actually, in 1994, when there were some conflicts and disagreements of opinion between President Karadzic and General Mladic, I do not know exactly the nature of those bad relations - but I would say that evidently it was about who was going to be the leader, and I say this in quotations, "the leader of the Serbian people" in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Because both men, both of them, enjoyed great respect and authority in the region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, General Krstic, if you did not agree with that speech because it did not correspond to reality, did you do anything to deny or correct the truth and to impose the truth?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That speech and mentioning me in the speech by President Karadzic is an absurdity. I didn't plan the operation; I didn't take part in the planning of the operation, just the realisation of the decisions of the Corps Commander with respect to the separation of the enclaves. Neither did I plan this and report about that to President Karadzic. That small operation which was to have been realised was the decision of the Corps Command, was approved by the Commander of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska and not the Supreme Commander. The Supreme Commanders does not direct operations in the operational sense but of strategic importance. I simply did not have occasion to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I'm sorry for interrupting you. We know that already. You spoke to us about that. But my question was: You accepted that for the public at large, and even for Republika Srpska, you accepted that you had planned and conducted the operation, and that is why I am asking you: What did you do to deny that, at least to render justice? Because if someone has merit, then that merit should be attributed to the right person. And after all, you let this pass and you accepted it; is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I did not accept that, but I did not deny it either. I didn't have the opportunity to do so. Quite simply, I did not dare do that because it was a question of the President of the Republic, the Supreme Commander. But it is well known whose merits it is of the operation. And the background of all that is, in fact, the relationship between those two men and not whether it was my merit or not. I don't know. He mentioned General Zivanovic as well with respect to Srebrenica and Zepa, but there was not a single word of mention made of General Mladic, although General Mladic led the whole operation, from the time the order for continuing the operation was received onwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question, General Krstic, and another topic. You explained that certain brigades refused to obey Mladic's order to march on Srebrenica on the 10th of July, and I think, my impression is, that you said that those brigades fled. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I do apologise, but I don't think that would be so. I didn't say at all that the brigades had fled and that they did not wish to carry out General Mladic's orders. It was only a question of the fact that the Commander of the Zvornik Brigade, Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic, at the meeting in Bratunac, told General Mladic, he said, "General, sir, we don't know where the 28th Division is," and the consequences to his brigade would be great unless measures were undertaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps you are right. Perhaps I misunderstood. But in any event, a Brigade Commander addresses himself to the Commander-in-Chief to say, "You see, sir, that will not be good." In a certain way, he is calling into question the orientation of the Commander-in-Chief. Having seen that, did you have the same opportunity after the meetings at the Fontana Hotel, after having learnt that there were hundreds and hundreds of people in Potocari who had nothing to eat or drink, and as you said once, knowing General Mladic, were you in a position to say to General Mladic, "General, be careful. Something serious could happen"? Because at Srebrenica some Brigade Commanders had refused General Mladic's order to advance on Srebrenica. So these two precedents, the meeting in Bratunac and in Srebrenica, you saw that there were people who were able to say to General Mladic, "Be careful. Pay attention to this." Were you not also in a position to say the same thing to General Mladic in relation to the evacuation of the population from Potocari?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe you had in mind when you were speaking about refusing orders, I assume you meant not to continue the attack on Srebrenica and Potocari. And there was a suggestion of this kind and the request that we do not move towards Potocari, and that is what we succeeded in doing, not to go to Potocari, because there were a lot of civilians there, refugees from the town of Srebrenica and the surrounding villages. So that is something we succeeded in doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Yes, General Krstic, and Mladic, in a certain sense, did reverse his position. General Mladic was a personality, therefore, who would accept suggestions even from a Brigade Commander. As for the Chief of Staff of the Corps, would he not have accepted a suggestion from you? And this is not a hypothetical, because you saw that General Mladic did retrace his steps. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, he too, after suggestions from the Brigade Commanders and the rest, came to realise that that order was nonsensical, that there was no need to move on towards Potocari, and that's why he accepted that. The Corps Commander, General Zivanovic, was there too and he was the first to have been the one, not only with respect to subsequent events after the entrance into Srebrenica, he should have been the one to tell the Commander when he ordered the continuation of the attack to Srebrenica, he should have said that that was not the objective of the operation. He did not do that, he did not do so. And I assumed that it was an attempt to demilitarise Srebrenica by taking weapons from members of the 28th Division and nothing else, nothing else at all. And he took on this responsibility when it came to the civilian population and the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us go on to another question now. You said that Kosoric did not follow you after you stopped at -- after you stopped at Potocari, we've spoken about that at length, and that you only asked him to report to you on the 13th of July, at the forward command post at Krivaca. My question: Why did you ask him to report to you? What was his task? What were the results that he was to report to you about?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do apologise, but I did not ask at all for any report from him. I did not ask him to report to me or submit a report of any kind. I didn't say that. I just said that he should report to me at the forward command post at Krivaca with respect to his presence in the area when it comes to the Zepa operation. He did not receive any assignment from me with respect to the evacuation of the population, and I am profoundly convinced that he did not receive that assignment from anyone else either. Because on the 13th, in the morning, he was at the forward command post of Krivaca, and he was with me throughout the rest of the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question: You explained that you were entrusted with the Zepa operation during the meeting at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters, and you said in that connection that the order required that they should regroup at Viogora, that the troops should regroup at Viogora. And you said the only unit entrusted with continuing the Srebrenica operation were those that depended directly on the Commander in Chief, that is, the 65th Protection Regiment, the 10th Sabotage Detachment, and the MUP forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic, at the meeting at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters, said that the 28th Division continued to be his concern and that the 65th Protection Regiment was present there, his battalion of the military police, the diversionary unit, and so on, and the detachment of the special MUP Brigade arrived too. That's what I said earlier on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And those troops remained under his direct command; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for sure, and I say this with full responsibility, that the battalion of the military police and the 10th Diversionary Unit was, throughout, under his command. I don't know whether the detachment of the special MUP was also under his command; that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in any event the order on the attack on Zepa, your order of the 13th of July, also mentions MUP forces as reserve forces. Those MUP forces mentioned in your order on the attack on Zepa, are they the same forces or other forces; that is, are they those same forces that are under the command of General Mladic or are they some other forces?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, they were not reserve MUP forces, they were the station units of MUP within the rear of the territory, west of Zepa, towards Kladanj. And I'm thinking, first and foremost, of the station units of MUP of the municipality of Han Pijesak, and co-action with those units is mentioned in preventing the possible operations of combat groups, units, from Zepa, of the BH army, towards Kladanj, with respect to the civilian population. Nothing else. So just co-action with those units. And they executed their customary, usual, regular tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Krstic, what were the regular duties of MUP forces?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was wartime and throughout the war the regular MUP tasks/duties were to see that law and order was enforced throughout the territory where there was no army, because the army was up at the front. And their focal task was to ensure security of the vital facilities, the facilities essential to life and work, the life and work of the people; to ensure security for those positions, such as communication, the waterworks and sewage system, and other things of that kind, which were important to the functioning of the system of authority in the republic. I apologise, Mr. President. The special MUP Brigade was a combat unit and was deployed in that manner by order of the Supreme Commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have stated that the 6th Protection Regiment, though it is not quoted in the order for the attack on Zepa, the order that we have been discussing, did participate in that attack because it was in the area. So the 6th Regiment [sic], was it attached to you? Did it come under your command?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, it is the infantry battalion that I spoke about, and I spoke about it at length, and the witness spoke about that today as well. It is the battalion which was in the area since the beginning of the conflict and it was engaged towards Zepa. They are people, elderly people. They were made up of elderly members. And when organising the operation towards Zepa, that battalion was at those positions and was, indeed, included in executing the tasks towards Zepa. They received their assignment from their superior commanding officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But, General Krstic, I think that my understanding was that this 6th Protection Regiment prevented you from passing through Potocari on the 12th of July. Was it deployed for both operations then?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, the 65th Protection Motorised Regiment was located in several localities in that part of Republika Srpska. Its command, with two more battalions, was engaged in offering security for the Main Staff of the army in Han Pijesak. One battalion was deployed towards Zepa as a combat unit continuously, and we mentioned that a moment ago. Then the battalion of the military police of the 65th Regiment was located in Nova Kasaba throughout, and part of the mechanicised Battalion of the 65th Protection Regiment. So the battalion of the military police was also doing security in Potocari, so that battalion of the military police had nothing to do whatsoever, no connection whatsoever, with the battalion that was deployed towards Zepa. The police battalion are elite troops which are deployed following orders from the Supreme Commander. This other battalion was where it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, General Krstic. So the operation launched against Zepa, as the Commander entrusted with the preparation and conduct of that operation, what were the measures that you envisaged to take in relation to civilians and prisoners of war which you might capture in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the whole, we fully applied the provisions from the existing rules and regulations and the Geneva Conventions when it comes to the civilian population of Zepa and the prisoners of war, and I am thinking of members of Zepa Brigade within the compositions of the 28th Division, and we did not deviate from that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But what are the measures that you envisaged in the planning and the implementation of the Zepa operation? What measures did you make provision for?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The complete protection -- complete protection for the civilian population, and nobody was allowed to do anything against that. And when it came to prisoners of war, we applied procedures that were prescribed for the treatment of the prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, General, another question: The report of the United Nations Secretary-General indicates that General Mladic informed UNPROFOR, on the 19th of July, at 1330 hours, that the Zepa enclave had fallen and that it was necessary to organise transport for the civilian population towards territory controlled by the government. My question is the following: Were you informed from the beginning of the operation that an evacuation plan, a large-scale evacuation plan for civilians needed to be executed once the enclave was captured?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The negotiations, when it came to the evacuation of the population, that was done by the Main Staff. I was not involved in that. I don't know how General Mladic could have informed anyone that on the 19th of July, the enclave of Zepa had fallen when that is not true. Perhaps he was able to draw this conclusion from the negotiations at the time which he had with the representatives of the authorities from Zepa, and the representatives of the army from Zepa. But the Zepa enclave fell far later, at the end of July, 1st of August. It is true that the civilians had been evacuated earlier on from the area; that's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But, General, you planned the Zepa operation and you were in command of the Zepa operation. Being in that position, did you know in advance how many buses and other things would be needed to evacuate the local population? Because the objective of the Zepa operation was to capture Zepa and there were civilians there, the population. So you, as the planner of that operation, you should have envisaged a whole series of measures to deal with that situation. Did you envisage how many buses, what quantity of supplies you would need for the population? Why did Mladic appear here when you were the responsible person? Mladic told you, "You go there and I'm going to the other side, in another direction."

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole business around the refugees was done by the Main Staff, headed by General Mladic. They were in charge of everything. They conducted negotiations with the representatives of the civilian authorities, the army. We had not planned the evacuation of the population. The objective was just to disarm the Zepa Brigade and not to evacuate the population as well. General Mladic succeeded in arriving at an agreement for the evacuation of the population and he ensured the necessary number of buses and decided upon the route that the buses were to take in evacuating the population, and which measures were to be undertaken when the population was leaving Zepa on territory under Serb control, and their further transport onwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, General Krstic, and I'm sorry for interrupting again. Are you telling us that General Mladic, when he ordered you to go on Zepa, did he tell you at a certain point in time, "Disarm the Zepa Brigade, that is your task. The civilian population, that is my problem." Did he tell you that at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in that sense, he didn't say it in that sense. He said what is written in the order. And I was in command of the army against the Zepa Brigade, and everything else was his concern, and what he did later on with respect to the evacuation of the population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So according to what you say, we are now focusing on General Mladic. As you know, General Mladic also insisted, within the framework of the negotiations on Zepa, that men between 18 and 55 years of age should surrender. Does his speech resemble the one he made at the Fontana Hotel within the framework of the Srebrenica operation? Did that mean that all the men in this age group were considered to be combatants?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all of them should have been considered combatants. Men until the age of 16 or men over the age of 60, they should not have been considered combatants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I should now like to go on to some more practical issues, if I may call them that. What was the size of the territory in square kilometres that came under the jurisdiction of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say now and express it in square kilometres. But how big the area is, all I can tell you -- I can just give you the borders of it, of the zone of responsibility of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That won't be necessary. My question has to do with the fact that there is a lot of difficulty in learning about things, but I had the impression that the territory was smaller than one would have us believe.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, the territory was vast, it was a large territory; in the south, stretching towards Gorazde; in the north, to between Zvornik and Janja; to the west, up to Kladanj, Olovo, and Vares; and to the east, to the River Drina. That is an enormous territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think there's any point. I can understand that for you it was an enormous area. But when we say that a territory is large or small, we must know the size. But never mind, you don't know that and perhaps you don't need to know that. We won't insist on the matter any further.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is large for the simple reason that the Drina Corps did not have as many members, for example, as the 1st Krajina Corps, which had over 50.000 men within it. The Drina Corps had at the most about 18.000 men, and the territory was vast, as I say, so everything was -- all the men were engaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to go back to another question, General Krstic. When you planned the Zepa operation, you had to use a whole series of information regarding the 28th Division or the Zepa Brigade, et cetera. What was the information that you used to plan the operation?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Information, we had to -- when it comes to information, we had to bear in mind a lot of factors; first of all, the terrain itself where the operation was to have taken place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for that you had a map, a map giving you the configuration of the terrain. But information about the effectives of the 28th Division, specifically the Zepa Brigade, the quantity of weapons, what possibilities they had of movement. I don't know. I'm not a military man, but I think in order to plan a certain operation, you need information. So my question is: What were your sources of information?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to the Zepa Brigade, we treated it like any other brigade within the composition of the 28th Division. It did, in fact, cover a far greater region on the Zepa territory, greater than any other brigade of the 28th Division located on the -- in the territory of Srebrenica. The land afforded effective defence because of the configuration of the terrain itself. It was far easier to defend yourself in a region of that kind than it was to attack, because the terrain is like that with many channels -- cut across with many channels and so on, so that it was very good for defence purposes. And when it comes to weapons, it was armed like any other armed brigade from the composition of the 28th Division. They had infantry weapons, and pieces -- calibres ranging up to 120-millimetres. And when I say 120-millimetres, I'm thinking of mortars. Furthermore, we also made assessments and thought that it was possible that a greater number of people from Srebrenica, in one way or another, had crossed into that area, and so that that brigade, when it comes to manpower, had been reinforced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to go a little further, General Krstic. Did you have the chance of having information obtained, if I can say so, from the enemy in order to be able to plan the operation?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that time we had no information from the BH army forces from the Zepa region. We did not have any. We just had some information which was collected up until the time the offensive was undertaken towards Zepa, and those came from the units which were in contact with the forces -- with the Zepa forces on the line before the attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To go even further, did the VRS intercept radio communications by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether it did intercept or not, the telephone lines, and I don't know what the facilities were of that unit -- of the units of the 28th Division, what they had to intercept radio communication. When it comes to the Zepa Brigade, we at that time really didn't have any information that we received through intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, General, I'm sorry for interrupting again. To be more direct, I can accept that you did not know what resources and equipment they had, but can you admit that the VRS did use information that was intercepted -- the intercepted radio communications among the BH army?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally, as Brigade Commander, I was the Brigade Commander, and when I was, I did not have any information received through intercepts, nor was my brigade in a position to have -- it didn't have that kind of communications devices to carry out these intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as the Chief of Staff and later as the Corps Commander?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the Corps Commander and Chief of Staff, I said that I was there for a short space of time; I performed that function for a short space of time.
