The first document I saw was the one I saw here presented as evidence from the leader of the radio reconnaissance unit of the Drina Corps, which was obtained through intercepting conversations. But I still feel that that is highly unreliable information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Krstic, I have finished with my questions. I don't know whether my colleagues have any additional questions to put to you. Thank you very much, General Krstic, for having clarified a few points that we had to ask you about. You have just completed your testimony; I think you now need a rest. We're going to have a short break of 15 minutes which will allow us to bring in another witness, Mr. Petrusic, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence does have a witness who will testify without any protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we'll have a 15 --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. President. I think before we bring in the witness we should deal with the documents, because we have come to the end of General Krstic's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and there are many of them, I think. Okay. That's a good suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or it has just occurred to me that perhaps we can try to coordinate views with the Prosecution first before we address the matter in court, in the course of the day, this afternoon perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, perhaps. I think there are very many documents. Does the Prosecution agree with this suggestion of Mr. Petrusic? Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. We've had discussions previously, but we are quite happy to engage in additional discussions on these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll now have a 15-minute break. I should like to ask the registrar to bring in the witness, to have him in court when we come back to the courtroom. Fifteen minutes, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are now going to read the solemn declaration handed to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated, and try and get yourself comfortable and relax. You are now going to be answering questions put to you by Mr. Petrusic, and then you will be answering questions from the Prosecution and possibly from the Judges. But Mr. Petrusic will start. Your witness, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President. Examined by Mr. Petrusic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, will you introduce yourself, please? Give us your name and surname.

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Milanko Radulovic, born on the 12th of January, 1961, in the village of Kusace, in the municipality of Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have completed secondary schooling?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm an electrician by profession.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you work?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I work in Han Pijesak, where I live with my family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, I have told you this before, I think, but please try and make pauses between my question and your answer. Wait for 10 to 15 seconds, please, before you give us your answer because everything is being interpreted and the interpreters have to do their work, and it's difficult to know what the question is and what the answer is if we hurry. Mr. Radulovic, tell us, please, you're married, you're a family man.

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us where you were at the beginning of the armed conflict in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Where did you find yourself in 1992? But just slowly, nice and slowly, please, with breaks in between.

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: In Han Pijesak, my native town, I lived there with my family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you join the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: I joined the army at the beginning of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the beginning of April, that was the former Yugoslav People's Army, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was the former Yugoslav People's Army, and it was the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. unit -- I joined up in a unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what unit? Be more specific, please.

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: It was the unit which was composed of local inhabitants. And at the beginning of the war, they took up positions in the surrounding villages in the municipality of Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it have a name of any kind, that unit?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: When the JNA withdrew, it came under the 1st Romanija Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as a member of the 1st Romanija Brigade, you were sent to what position? Just give us a pause.

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: We went to Han Pijesak, the position there, the village of Jelovci, Borovine. The village of Jelovci, Borovine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that near Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: From that village to Zepa, it is approximately 20 kilometres. But the Muslim villages were closer by, Stoborane, Plane, Borovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were with your unit in the village of Jelovci and Borovine; and on the other side, opposite those villages, as you have said, there was Plane, Podgora, Pozeplje, and that was where the members of the Muslim army were.

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, that is to say, the summer of 1992, were there any conflicts between your unit and the members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, at those positions, at the positions you held?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: Not at first, no. Up until the beginning of June, the units from the area around Plane, I don't know what the name of that unit was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We couldn't follow what the witness was saying. Could he repeat that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So those were the only conflicts at that time, during the summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: There was a conflict on the 7th of August, when the village of Borovine was attacked, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, by the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the village of Borovine was inhabited by a civilian population, or was it an entrenched military position?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was the civilian population, and a portion of the army was there too, as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just a second. What kind of civilian population was in the village of Borovine?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, you heard the question by Judge Riad. Would you try and answer the question? Which civilian population was located in the village of Borovine?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the local inhabitants, the people who live in that village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And their ethnicity was?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: It was Serbian. They were of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Completely Serb, or composed of several ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, they were only Serbs, exclusively Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know that at the beginning -- that is to say, in the spring of 1993, a safe area of Zepa was formed.

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time were you still a member of the 1st Romanija Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not. We were the 65th Protection Regiment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your unit continue to hold the position as a unit of the 65th Protection Regiment?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We know that the 65th Protection Regiment had several battalions. Could you tell us what your battalion was at that position?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: It was the infantry battalion, composed of younger and older people. The ages ranged from 25 to 50.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we then say that the members of that infantry battalion were mostly local inhabitants of Han Pijesak or, rather, the environs of Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were the inhabitants of Han Pijesak and the surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The positions around the protected zone, the safe area, of Zepa, was that held by your battalion alone, that infantry battalion of the 65th Regiment, or were there other units there as well?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: My battalion held the region of Borovac, Godjenje, and Pozeplje --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat that last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: The Biretic Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic, in addition to your own unit, what other units held the position around Zepa? Just make pauses, please.

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: The Rogaticka Brigade held that position in addition to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Rogaticka Brigade, is that its usual name? But as to establishment and formation of the Drina Corps, it was the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Radulovic, in July 1995, where were you and your unit located? Please make pauses. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: In July 1995, I was located at Ocadzalo Sarajevo, and part of the men from three companies, about 40 people, went to Kosara.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So part of the men from your battalion was transferred at an earlier period to a place called Ocadzalo, in the region, that is to say, the zone of responsibility, of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From there, the Ocadzalo place, did you return to the Zepa area?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: I returned to the Zepa area on the 15th of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following whose orders? On whose orders did your unit reach the Zepa area on the 15th of July? Pursuant to whose orders?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to the order of the Commander of the Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the Battalion Commander at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: Radivojevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have a rank?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He was a major.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in the Zepa area you arrived on the 15th of July, when combat operations started; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's when I got there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who led, that is to say, commanded, the operation at Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: When I got there, I heard from the people who were already there that General Krstic was in command of the operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know which duty, which post, General Krstic held at the time in the command of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: General Krstic at that time performed the function of Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, until the end of the operation at Zepa, with your unit, stay in that locality? Did you remain there?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the combat, who issued orders to you, to your unit?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: We received orders from the company leader and Battalion Commander; the Battalion Commander would issue orders to the company leader and he would issue orders to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether your battalion, the infantry battalion of the 65th Protection Regiment, at that time, whether it was attached to the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't think it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why don't you think it was?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: Because the Protection Regiment belonged to the command of the Main Staff. It received orders from the Battalion Commander and company leader.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In those combat operations which took place, your battalion, quite naturally, had its left and right neighbour, as they say in the army; is that true?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you happen to know who was one of your neighbours, one of those two neighbours?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: On the one side there was the Drina Corps, and we were on the right. It was to the left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who commanded that left flank?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. It was a little further off from us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During those combat operations, did you and your unit have any prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: My unit had two prisoners, and we turned them over to the battalion command. Later on I heard that they were exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about -- whether it was talked about, whether people said that some Muslims had disappeared, that Muslim soldiers, in fact, had disappeared from the Zepa area?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I didn't hear anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you remain at Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: I remained -- we remained at Zepa until the 15th of August, thereabouts. The 15th or the 20th of August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: After that my unit withdrew; that is to say, we went home for a rest, and then we went to Herzegovina, to the battlefront there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your battalion command still -- at that time did it still issue orders on the basis of which you acted?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: At the end of August, we passed over to the 1st Romanija Brigade. The unit, at the end of August, joined the 2nd Romanija Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As I understood it, it was transformed to become the 2nd Romanija Brigade; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Petrusic. I see Mr. McCloskey about to rise. Mr. Radulovic, you will now be answering questions put to you by the Prosecution. Cross-examined by Mr. McCloskey:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Radulovic.

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 65th Protection Regiment, you were in that regiment for how long?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: I was in it from May 1993 until August 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your position and rank at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: I had the rank of a regular soldier, a private.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your job was as an infantryman, carrying a rifle?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many other battalions were in the 65th Protection Regiment in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly; I don't know the exact number. There was a police battalion. I don't know by heart the establishment. I wasn't an officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever get together and have reunions with your old unit?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: We did meet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did that include other battalions besides your infantry battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: No. Other people from outside the area were in those units whom I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever get together with the people from the other battalions?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: I probably did, but rarely. I didn't know them. They were not locals; they were from other parts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1995, where was the military police battalion located?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know of a group that was in the area of Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear of the 65th Protection Regiment being involved in the Srebrenica operation, or the operation shortly after Srebrenica in the area of Nova Kasaba and Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: At the time of the fall of Srebrenica, I was at Ocadzalo, near Sarajevo. So on the 15th of July, I came to the positions in Zepa. So I didn't know, I wasn't aware of these things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever heard about the 65th Protection Regiment, your regiment, being involved in any activities after the fall of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: Which enclave?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. I'm not familiar with any such information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear of any casualties, any of the people from the 65th Regiment that were killed in actions with the Muslim column fleeing from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you or did you not hear of any members of your regiment being killed?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: I did not. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Fouad Riad? Yes, Judge Wald. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I just have one question, Mr. Radulovic. During the period that you were up in the vicinity of Zepa, between July 15th and the time that you left, August 15th, did you ever hear any rumours, allegations, charges, gossip, anything dealing with Muslim prisoners or members of the Muslim column being executed or killed when they were going toward Tuzla from Srebrenica? Did you ever hear any -- no matter where, over the radio, TV, other soldiers, even if you didn't think they were true. During the period you were in Zepa, July to August.

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: I heard that information about Srebrenica when I returned from Herzegovina, that something had happened there, when the campaign started against --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And when would that be, approximately. The date, the month, whenever.

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: Beginning of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Radulovic, how did you learn about that information regarding the events of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: I learnt about that on television. When I returned from Herzegovina, I saw reports on television. I can't express myself. I heard about these people who had been accused of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you heard this on television, did people speak amongst themselves about what they saw on television?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There were comments in cafes, squares, restaurants, homes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you have the impression that all the people had learnt about this only after that date, or were there people who said, "I already knew about this before"?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: Some people did know from earlier on, but I learnt about them later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What did those people say, both groups?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO RADULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. They were saying that something had happened. No one knew exactly what had happened and what the official report was. That was just on television at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Radulovic, you have completed your testimony here at the International Criminal Tribunal. We thank you very much for coming here, and we wish you a safe journey to your home. I'm going to ask the usher to accompany you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that everyone is waiting for this moment to have a break, I think. Mr. Visnjic, you have something to say before we break?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, for after the break, we have prepared the next witness, but the Registry has cautioned me that perhaps it would be advisable to propose protective measures for this witness. He has requested a pseudonym, distortion of face and voice. So I have been advised that we should make that request before the break so that the technical services can prepare for the protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Perhaps we should go into private session to discuss the reasons for this request for protective measures. Mr. Registrar. We apologise to the public, but we have to go into private session and that means that there can be no people in the public gallery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness DE. Can you hear me well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are now going to read the solemn declaration which the usher is going to hand to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. We're not getting any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be able to hear the witness without voice distortion, it is necessary to use channel 7. So there is a small technical problem that needs to be addressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Now I can hear the English booth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as for the French booth, is everything all right? Yes. And the B/C/S booth? Yes. And as for the counsel, Mr. Petrusic, is everything all right for you? Can you follow?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm getting the English or, rather, the B/C/S, but I am hearing it on channel 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is everything all right for you, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, everything is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask General Krstic whether he is able to follow the discussion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's fine. So we can continue now. The usher is going to show you a piece of paper, Witness DE, on which your name should be written. And please tell us, yes or no, whether that is, indeed, your name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. So you will now be answering questions which, I think it is, Mr. Visnjic is going to put to you. Mr. Visnjic, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, to begin with I would like to ask the witness a few questions regarding his personal particulars, so I would suggest that we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let us go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session now, Mr. Visnjic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE, will you tell us what duties you took over after February 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: After this date I took up duty as Commander of the Engineers Battalion of the Drina Corps, which was in the process of establishment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you take up that duty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: I do not have the exact date, but I reckon it was about a month after I handed over these duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain to Their Honours, what does this Engineers Battalion in the process of formation actually mean? It is rather unusual.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: It means that in formal and legal terms, from the moment I signed the report on the handing over of duty, and when I received an order on my appointment, I was the Commander of the Engineers Battalion. In legal terms, I was legally liable, and everything that I was entitled to as a Battalion Commander in terms of rights and obligations came into effect. However, these words "in the process of establishment," meant that actually I was my own Commander, because there was no unit. And roughly up to the time of the events we will be discussing, I managed to form a unit with a strength of roughly one engineers platoon in the combat element and two platoons as non-combat elements, which means a total of some 90 men under my command from then on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said combat and non-combat sections. Could you explain that? What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Combat elements are those that we used in combat operations and which were fully fit and capable of carrying out combat operations; and the other part of the unit consisted of people who were of lower combat capacities but who could serve to carry out certain engineering works and tasks. The combat element numbered 21 pioneers and about 10 or so operators of engineering machinery. Those were the people who went into the area of combat activities, where the combat was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was envisaged according to establishment for the Corps engineers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: The armies that were in the process of being established in the former Yugoslavia after it was dissolved mostly used the rules and regulations that they had inherited from the former JNA. The Drina Corps was also supposed to use the Rules of Service of the Corps, and according to those Rules of Service, it was regulated that the Corps should have a Chief of Engineering, Engineering Units, an Engineers Platoon, and a Pontoon Bridge Battalion. But due to the situation in the Corps area in terms of lack of resources and the problems with engineering activities, and because of the inability to find manpower, and because of quite developed brigade engineers units, we decided to form an Engineers Battalion that was taken out of the division as a formation. But as we had the Drina River as an obstacle on which we carried out certain activities, and this fits within the area of pontoon bridge construction work, we made some changes there. So we tried to include a part of that Pontoon Bridge Unit. As we had a large number of engineering works in the area of the Corps' responsibility, we formed a Construction Unit which mostly engaged in construction work and which, according to establishment, does not belong to engineers units at this level. You come across such units for the first time at the strategic level of organisation. So much about the structure of these units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, that meant that you just had the nucleus of the special separate services and branches, that is to say, you were endeavouring, up until the summer of 1995, to develop those nuclei from which that Corps -- which to allow you to have full manpower later on. Am I right in saying so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to ask the usher to show the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid, Mr. President, we once again have to move into private session for this next document because the document identifies the witness. It is 404, Prosecution Exhibit 404, 318. Exhibit 404, 318 footnote. For purposes of the record, it was 404, footnote 188.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us move into private session now, please, to be able to place the document on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, you may continue. We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the previous exhibit that you have just seen, is one of the ways in which you supplied -- that is to say, formed, established your unit, was it precisely supplying it with materiel and technical devices from the subordinate units of the brigade? Did they give over part of their equipment to your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Well, in addition to this, let me go back to what you asked me a moment ago when you asked me who I referred to, and then I could continue from there. Our army functioned according to two basic principles: The principle of having one command and the principle of subordination. One command meant that every person in the chain of command above him has only one man who can issue orders to him, one superior; and the principle of subordination implied that the subordinated persons must act on the orders of their superior unless an order of that kind represented a criminal act, which was regulated in other rules and regulations positive. So for me, the superior was the Commander of the Drina Corps. However, the Commander of the Drina Corps had the right to authorise somebody else to command in his name, on his behalf, in certain situations. And in this concrete case, this authorisation was given to the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps. So that I frequently reported in the daily reports and information, I would report to the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps. The document that was presented to me speaks of the method and way in which I attempted to establish the Engineers Battalion; that is to say, upon arrival in the Drina Corps, the Commander of the Drina Corps and the Chief of Staff, I would tell them -- present my concept of how I wanted to form the battalion. This was accepted and I went into action; I went to work to establish it. The essence for my concept and idea for its formation, as I did not have any other sources, was to tour the brigades, the engineering departments of the brigades, and to ask them for the materiel and technical resources that I needed, the manpower and everything else that I needed to form a battalion. One of the means -- one of the ways in which I came by what you saw, what was mentioned in the document, a moment ago, that was my attempt, but nothing came of it. I went back disillusioned because I wasn't able to do what I had planned. In the meantime, the Corps Commander decided that 21 soldiers, who were being trained in the Zvornik Brigade, be given to me to train them and to become those 21 pioneers, and that is how we actually started forming this Corps. And it was the core of the future pioneer company, the nucleus of the future pioneer company. That's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One more question. Let us repeat for the purposes of the record: Is it true that probably the only resources -- the only thing you got was the truck that was mentioned in the document, because it said in the transcript that you didn't get anything. Just that one truck; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: As far as I remember, that was the only resource -- piece of equipment we received. Engineering and passenger vehicles, that's another matter. That is something large.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the engineers unit of the Drina Corps was to be a strong unit. But in the spring of 1995 -- I apologise. Just one moment. I'll continue. I apologise. In the spring of 1995, although it was supposed to be a serious, strong unit formation-wise, the engineers unit of the Drina Corps was still a fledgling organisation under formation and did not have within its composition what the regulations provide for with regard to manpower and the materiel and technical equipment; is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes, that is true; that is to say, for the most part, we had succeeded in forming nuclei from which we thought we would develop units from later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will the usher now show the witness Exhibit 160/4 and 160/1. It is a Prosecution exhibit -- two Prosecution exhibits. Mr. President, perhaps we can use our copies, make our copies available to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 160/1, that will be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have before you, sir, a satellite image used by the Prosecution in presenting evidence in its part of the proceedings. Please focus on the sector marked A, the A section.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On this section you can see heavy vehicles, trucks. I think you can see four of them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I'd like to ask the usher to place, straight after this, Exhibit 160/4. It's the same aerial image but from a different angle. 160/4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, are these the vehicles that were to be found in the location of Konjevic Polje in 1995 and 1996 --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- when these two exhibits were made?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As opposed to what we discussed earlier on, on this particular picture, 160/4, this appears to be a serious base of materiel and technical equipment. Could you explain to the Trial Chamber what these vehicles are and what their purpose was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: What you have seen in the two documents shown are a launching bridge, heavy launching bridge, on the Kras type of vehicle. In Konjevic Polje, it was brought from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps to Konjevic Polje. It was brought by the crew of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, the crew that knew how to handle it and work with this vehicle. And these vehicles never moved from this locality, this spot, until the NATO-pact aviation targeted the bridge at Rogatica. That was the first time when these -- that these vehicles were moved from here and taken to that locality to launch the bridge, launch a bridge. For them to be moved, I had to call the same crew from the SRK to move the vehicles. By establishment, this bridge should have been in the core, but quite obviously we didn't have the crew necessary for that kind of bridge, to man the bridge. Now, why was it here at all? Let me explain that locality of Konjevic Polje, if I may.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I have a set of questions relating to Konjevic Polje later on, and we're nearing the end of today's proceedings. Let me just ask you: Can you tell us when those vehicles arrived in the region of Konjevic Polje? When was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: I can't tell you the exact time, but since their arrival and were parked there, they never moved there except one excursion when the crew arrived to take them to the Rogatica area to launch the bridge at the spot where NATO strikes had destroyed a bridge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long? Give us a time frame.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Well, quite a long time. I don't know. I don't think time is important. But they were there for rather a long period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The exchange is going back and forth so quickly, Your Honour, I'm not getting everything that's being said. If we could slow it down, I'd appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is an indication of the general character of the work the interpreters have to do when you speak so quickly. Witness, you can't hear the interpreters, but they do exist, let me assure you. They're like God; they're there but we don't see them. So just bear in mind that between you, yourself, and Mr. Visnjic we have an interpreter. So please slow down and make pauses. Please continue, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think our time is up, perhaps, and we could slow down for good for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think that's a very good suggestion, and then you can organise your questions a little better, perhaps. Witness DE, we're going to stop there for today and continue tomorrow at 9.20 with your testimony. So we'll meet again tomorrow.
